book_intro: The book of Jeremiah is set during the politically tumultuous times following the fall of the Assyrians and the rise of the Babylonians. During Jeremiah's life, several groups of Judeans were deported to Babylon and the temple was destroyed. Though the precise boundaries of Judea and the surrounding regions during this period are difficult to determine, they likely resembled those that previously existed under Assyrian rule, with the exception that Edom (Idumea) was now the area formerly belonging to southern Judah.

passages.title: Restoration for Judah and Israel.
passages.text: The book now turns to positive themes. At last Jeremiah may “build and plant” (1:10). He claims that God will restore the nation (ch. 30), make a new covenant with Israel (ch. 31), bring Israel back to the Promised Land (ch. 32), and honor his covenant with David (ch. 33).

notes.text: second time . . . in the court of the guard. See 32:1–2.
God the Creator (10:16; 32:17), who formed and established the earth, makes the promises that follow. His word was as powerful in Jeremiah’s time as in Gen. 1:1–2:3. His promises cannot fail.
hidden things. Future things that God will now reveal.
God reveals that all current efforts to repel Babylon will fail. Because of Jerusalem’s evil deeds, God will fill it with dead bodies.
God promises health and healing for Jerusalem’s “wounds”—its devastation, disgrace, and sin (30:16–17; see 33:7–8)—but first he will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin.
Jerusalem has become a warning for other nations (see 15:4; 24:9; 29:18), but in the future it will be a testimony to God’s goodness.

voice of gladness. Jeremiah correctly prophesied that joy would cease when Jerusalem was made desolate (7:34; 16:9; 25:10). But now he prophesies that joy will be restored, with worship being the most important joy (30:19; Ps. 107:22; 136:1–26).
Branch. The Davidic messianic offspring (see Isa. 4:2; Zech. 3:8; 6:12). execute justice and righteousness. A key role God and his Messiah will play (Isa. 9:7; 11:5; Jer. 23:5–6; see 22:3; 13; 15).
The Messiah’s coming will mean salvation for Judah and Jerusalem. The city will be so changed that it will be called: “The Lord is our righteousness,” the name given to the Messiah in 23:6.

See 31:35–37. Like the new covenant, God’s covenant with David and Levi will endure forever. This does not contradict the NT teaching about a new covenant (31:31), for Christ fulfills the promise that one of David’s descendants will always reign over the house of Israel.

Like Abraham’s descendants, the offspring of David will be too many to be counted (Gen. 15:1–6), for there will be many believers in the Messiah. They will share the Messiah’s inheritance (Rom. 8:17).
